questions.title: Spring Kafka Setup and KafkaTemplate
questions.question: How do you set up Spring Kafka and use KafkaTemplate for sending messages?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- spring-kafka dependency + spring.kafka.* auto-configuration
- KafkaTemplate<K,V>: Spring abstraction over Kafka producer
- send() returns CompletableFuture<SendResult<K,V>> — async with partition + offset info
- @KafkaListener: consumer annotation — topic, groupId, concurrency
- @EnableKafka: enables listener container factory processing
- ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory: concurrency, ack mode, error handling
- Serialization: Spring JSON serializers for automatic object serialization

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Kafka provides a KafkaTemplate abstraction similar to JdbcTemplate. It handles serialization and producer lifecycle, exposing a clean API for sending messages. The send method returns a CompletableFuture for async success/failure handling without blocking.

On the consumer side, @KafkaListener works like @RabbitListener — annotate a method with the topic and consumer group, and Spring handles polling, deserialization, and offset management. Spring Boot auto-configures everything from your application.yml.

You write custom bean configuration mainly when you need multiple producer configurations — different serializers for different topics, or different error handling per listener.

questions.title: Kafka Delivery Semantics
questions.question: What are Kafka's delivery semantics and how do you achieve exactly-once processing?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- At-most-once: ack before processing — possible message loss, no duplicates
- At-least-once: ack after processing — no loss, possible duplicates
- Exactly-once: idempotent producer + transactional API — no loss, no duplicates
- Idempotent producer: enable.idempotence=true — broker deduplicates retried messages
- Kafka transactions: atomic produce+consume+produce — all or nothing
- Practical EOS: complex + lower throughput — prefer at-least-once + idempotent consumer

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kafka offers three delivery guarantees. At-most-once commits offset before processing — if the app crashes before processing, the message is lost. At-least-once commits after processing — no lost messages but possible redelivery if a crash occurs after processing but before commit. Exactly-once uses transactions to atomically produce and commit offset — zero loss, zero duplicates.

True exactly-once requires Kafka transactions. The idempotent producer deduplicates retried messages at the broker. Combined with the transactional API, you atomically consume a message, process it, and produce results — either all happens or none does.

In practice most teams use at-least-once with idempotent consumers — design handlers to be safe to process twice. This is simpler, performs better, and covers most use cases.

questions.title: Kafka Topic Design and Partition Strategy
questions.question: How do you design Kafka topics, decide partition count, and manage topics for a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Partitions: unit of parallelism — more partitions = more consumers = more throughput
- Replication factor: 3 for production (leader + 2 replicas) — survives 2 broker failures
- Retention: time-based (days/hours) or size-based retention of messages
- Compaction: keep only latest message per key — good for state/lookup topics
- Topic naming convention: domain.entity.event — orders.created, payments.processed
- Partition count: set based on expected max consumers × safety margin — hard to reduce later
- NewTopic @Bean: Spring Kafka creates topics if they don't exist on startup
- min.insync.replicas: ensure durability — acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Partition count is the most important design decision for a Kafka topic because it can only increase, never decrease. Set it based on your maximum anticipated consumer throughput. If you think you'll never need more than 6 parallel consumers for a topic, set it to 6. Adding more later is possible but rebalancing impacts are disruptive.

For production, always use a replication factor of 3 — one leader and two replicas. Combined with min.insync.replicas=2 and acks=all, this ensures a message is only acknowledged after it's written to at least two brokers. A single broker failure doesn't lose data.

Topic naming should follow a consistent pattern like domain.entity.event. This makes it easy to set access control policies — a service can be allowed to produce to its own domain's topics and consume from others. Compacted topics are a special case: they retain only the latest message per key, making them suitable for maintaining a current-state view of entities.

questions.title: Transactional Outbox Pattern with Kafka
questions.question: What is the transactional outbox pattern and how do you implement it with Kafka and Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Problem: database write and Kafka publish are two separate systems — no distributed transaction
- Two-phase commit: impractical at scale — locks, coordination overhead
- Outbox pattern: write event to database outbox table in same DB transaction as business data
- Polling publisher: separate process reads outbox table and publishes to Kafka, then deletes/marks published
- Debezium: CDC-based outbox relay — captures DB transaction log changes and publishes to Kafka
- Guarantees: at-least-once delivery — exactly-once requires idempotent consumers
- Spring Modulith: built-in support for event persistence and outbox pattern

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem. When you save business data and then publish to Kafka in two separate operations, either one can fail independently — leaving your system in an inconsistent state. Kafka also doesn't participate in database transactions, so you can't use a two-phase commit.

The solution is to write the Kafka event as a row in an outbox table in the same database transaction as your business data. Either both the order row and the outbox event row are committed, or neither is. Then a separate process reads pending outbox entries and publishes them to Kafka.

Debezium is the most robust implementation of the outbox publisher. It reads PostgreSQL's write-ahead log using Change Data Capture, eliminating the need to poll and the risk of missed events. When Debezium publishes the outbox row change to Kafka, you get reliable exactly-once event publication from the database change itself.

questions.title: Kafka Monitoring and Performance Tuning
questions.question: What are the key Kafka metrics to monitor and how do you tune performance for a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Consumer lag: most important metric — how far behind is consumer from latest offset
- spring.kafka.listener.idle-event-interval: detect idle consumers
- Micrometer integration: Spring Kafka exposes metrics automatically
- Producer metrics: record-send-rate, request-latency-avg, record-error-rate
- Consumer metrics: records-consumed-rate, fetch-latency-avg, commit-latency-avg
- batch.size + linger.ms: producer batching for higher throughput
- compression.type: lz4 or snappy for high-volume topics
- max.poll.records: how many records consumer fetches per poll

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Consumer lag is the most critical Kafka metric — it measures how far behind your consumer is from the latest message in a topic. A growing lag means your consumer can't keep up with production rate. Alert when lag exceeds a threshold that would affect business SLAs — for example, if your consumer is 10 minutes behind on the orders topic, orders are sitting unprocessed.

For producer performance, batch.size and linger.ms control how messages are grouped before sending. Increasing these improves throughput at the cost of slightly higher latency. For a high-volume topic, enabling lz4 compression reduces network bandwidth and storage significantly — typically 3-5x compression ratio for JSON payloads.

Spring Boot with Micrometer automatically exposes Kafka consumer and producer metrics to your metrics system. The consumer group lag can be monitored via Kafka's own consumer group metrics or through the Kafka Admin API, integrated into your Grafana dashboard alongside application metrics.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Key Metrics to Monitor

```
Consumer Metrics:
  kafka.consumer.fetch-latency-avg      → time per fetch request
  kafka.consumer.records-consumed-rate  → messages/second processed
  kafka.consumer.records-lag            → lag per partition (MOST IMPORTANT)
  kafka.consumer.commit-latency-avg     → offset commit latency

Producer Metrics:
  kafka.producer.record-send-rate       → messages/second produced
  kafka.producer.record-error-rate      → failed sends/second (alert if > 0)
  kafka.producer.request-latency-avg    → round-trip time to broker
  kafka.producer.batch-size-avg         → batching efficiency

Broker Metrics (JMX or Prometheus JMX Exporter):
  kafka.server:type=BrokerTopicMetrics,name=MessagesInPerSec
  kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions  (alert if > 0)
  kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=ActiveControllerCount (alert if != 1)
```

## Producer Tuning

```yaml
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      batch-size: 65536         # 64KB batch — default 16KB; larger = better throughput
      properties:
        linger.ms: 5            # wait 5ms to accumulate batch — better batching
        compression.type: lz4   # compress batches — ~3-5x for JSON
        buffer.memory: 67108864 # 64MB producer buffer
```

## Consumer Tuning

```yaml
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      properties:
        max.poll.records: 500      # records per poll — default 500
        fetch.min.bytes: 1024      # wait until 1KB available — reduces poll frequency
        fetch.max.wait.ms: 500     # or 500ms — whichever comes first
        session.timeout.ms: 45000  # consumer considered dead after 45s
        heartbeat.interval.ms: 15000
```

## Lag Monitoring with Micrometer

```java
@Component
public class KafkaLagMonitor {

    private final KafkaAdmin kafkaAdmin;
    private final MeterRegistry meterRegistry;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30000)  // check every 30 seconds
    public void checkConsumerLag() {
        // Use AdminClient to get consumer group lag
        try (AdminClient client = AdminClient.create(kafkaAdmin.getConfigurationProperties())) {
            client.listConsumerGroupOffsets("my-service")
                .partitionsToOffsetAndMetadata()
                .thenAccept(offsets -> offsets.forEach((tp, offsetMeta) -> {
                    long lag = offsetMeta.offset(); // simplified — real lag = latest - committed
                    Gauge.builder("kafka.consumer.group.lag",
                            () -> lag,
                            n -> n)
                        .tag("topic", tp.topic())
                        .tag("partition", String.valueOf(tp.partition()))
                        .register(meterRegistry);
                }));
        }
    }
}
```

questions.title: KafkaTemplate and ProducerFactory Configuration
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configures KafkaTemplate when spring-kafka is on the classpath. Configure producers via spring.kafka.producer.* properties. For advanced needs, define a ProducerFactory bean with custom serializers and idempotence settings.

sections.title: KafkaTemplate Hides the Kafka Producer API Behind Spring Abstractions — But You Still Need to Understand What Happens Underneath
sections.content:
Spring Boot auto-configures a `KafkaTemplate` bean from `spring.kafka.producer.*` properties. You inject it and call `send()`. But the defaults are designed for safety, not performance — and understanding the underlying `ProducerFactory` configuration is what separates a developer who uses Kafka from one who operates it.

`KafkaTemplate.send()` is **asynchronous by default.** It returns a `CompletableFuture<SendResult>` (Spring Kafka 3.x). Messages are batched in memory and sent when the batch is full or `linger.ms` expires. Calling `.get()` on the future blocks until the broker acknowledges the write. Without `.get()`, you have **fire-and-forget semantics** — the message might fail silently.

The `ProducerFactory` creates the underlying Kafka `Producer` instances. By default, it creates a new producer per thread. For transactional producers, it pools them. The serializer configuration (`key-serializer`, `value-serializer`) is set at the factory level and determines how Java objects are converted to bytes for transmission to the broker and deserialized back on the consumer side.

sections.title: Critical Producer Properties and Their Impact on Reliability
sections.content:
**`acks`** controls durability guarantees. `acks=1` (default) means the leader acknowledged the write but replicas may not have it yet — leader failure before replication loses the message. **`acks=all`** waits for all in-sync replicas to acknowledge, providing the strongest guarantee. Pair with `min.insync.replicas=2` on the topic to ensure at least two replicas confirm.

**`retries`** (default: `Integer.MAX_VALUE` in modern clients) and **`delivery.timeout.ms`** (default: 120 seconds) control retry behavior. The producer retries failed sends within the delivery timeout. **`enable.idempotence=true`** (default since Kafka 3.0) prevents duplicate messages from retries — the broker deduplicates based on producer ID and sequence number.

**`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection`** defaults to 5. With idempotence enabled, the producer maintains ordering even with multiple in-flight requests because the broker rejects out-of-order writes. Without idempotence, multiple in-flight requests can cause message reordering during retries.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`KafkaTemplate` wraps the Kafka producer API with Spring abstractions. Auto-configured from `spring.kafka.producer.*` properties, you inject it and call `send()`.

`send()` is **asynchronous** — returns a `CompletableFuture`. Messages batch in memory and send when the batch is full or `linger.ms` expires. Without calling `.get()`, failures are silent.

The critical configuration is **`acks`**. Default `acks=1` means only the leader confirms — leader failure before replication loses the message. **`acks=all`** waits for all in-sync replicas, providing the strongest guarantee.

**Idempotence** (default since Kafka 3.0) prevents duplicates from retries using producer ID and sequence numbers.

The serializer choice (`StringSerializer`, `JsonSerializer`, Avro) is set at the `ProducerFactory` level.

In practice, I always set `acks=all`, verify `enable.idempotence=true`, and use `CompletableFuture` callbacks for error handling instead of fire-and-forget.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **KafkaTemplate.send() is asynchronous by default** — returns `CompletableFuture<SendResult>`; without calling `.get()` or adding a callback, send failures are silently ignored.
- **acks=1 only waits for the leader** — leader failure before replication loses the message; `acks=all` waits for all in-sync replicas and provides the strongest durability guarantee.
- **Idempotence is enabled by default since Kafka 3.0** — producer ID and sequence numbers prevent duplicate messages from retries; must be paired with `acks=all` and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5`.
- **ProducerFactory creates one producer per thread by default** — for transactional producers, it pools them; misconfiguring the pool size causes contention under load.
- **delivery.timeout.ms (default 120s) bounds total retry time** — the producer retries within this window; after expiry, the `CompletableFuture` completes exceptionally with a `TimeoutException`.

questions.question: How does @KafkaListener work? Explain partitions, consumer groups, and concurrency.
questions.title: @KafkaListener — Partitions, Consumer Groups, and Concurrency
questions.direct_answer: @KafkaListener creates a message-driven POJO consumer. Each listener is part of a consumer group; Kafka assigns partitions to consumers in the group. Concurrency = number of threads = max number of partitions that will be consumed in parallel.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of consumer group partition assignment and the concurrency-partition relationship
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting concurrency > number of partitions — extra threads are idle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain rebalancing when concurrency changes or instances scale, and the difference between group IDs for competing consumers vs fan-out

sections.title: @KafkaListener Runs on a Thread From a ConcurrentMessageListenerContainer — Not the Main Thread, Not a Web Thread
sections.content:
When you annotate a method with `@KafkaListener`, Spring Kafka creates a **`ConcurrentMessageListenerContainer`** that manages consumer threads. Each consumer thread polls Kafka, receives records, and invokes your listener method. This happens completely outside the web request lifecycle — no `HttpServletRequest`, no Spring MVC context.

The **`concurrency`** property controls how many consumer threads run. `@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", concurrency = "3")` creates 3 consumer instances, each assigned a subset of partitions. With 6 partitions and `concurrency=3`, each consumer handles 2 partitions. **Consumers beyond the partition count sit idle** — `concurrency=8` on a 6-partition topic wastes 2 threads.

The **`groupId`** determines which consumer group this listener belongs to. All listeners with the same `groupId` share the partitions of a topic. Different `groupId` values create independent consumers — each group gets all messages independently. This is how you have one group for order processing and another for analytics, both reading from the same topic without interfering with each other's offset management.

sections.title: Partition Assignment, Manual Assignment, and Consumer Thread Safety
sections.content:
By default, Kafka uses the **`RangeAssignor`** to distribute partitions. When consumers join or leave the group, a **rebalance** reassigns partitions. During rebalance, all consumers in the group pause — no messages are processed. With many partitions and frequent scaling, rebalances cause latency spikes.

The **`CooperativeStickyAssignor`** (recommended) performs incremental rebalances — only the affected partitions are reassigned, and other consumers continue processing. Configure with `spring.kafka.consumer.properties.partition.assignment.strategy=org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor`.

For fixed partition-to-consumer mapping, use `@KafkaListener(topicPartitions = @TopicPartition(topic = "orders", partitions = {"0", "1"}))`. This skips group management entirely — the consumer always reads from the specified partitions. Useful when partition ordering must map to specific processing logic.

**Listener methods are called on the consumer thread** — blocking operations (database writes, HTTP calls) block the consumer from polling. If the method takes longer than `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5 minutes), Kafka assumes the consumer is dead and triggers a rebalance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@KafkaListener` creates a `ConcurrentMessageListenerContainer` that manages consumer threads. These threads poll Kafka and invoke your listener method — completely outside the web request lifecycle.

**`concurrency`** controls consumer thread count. With 6 partitions and `concurrency=3`, each consumer handles 2 partitions. Consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.

**`groupId`** determines partition sharing. Same group = partitions distributed. Different groups = each gets all messages. This is how you have separate processing and analytics consumers on the same topic.

Partition assignment uses `RangeAssignor` by default. **`CooperativeStickyAssignor`** is better — incremental rebalances instead of stop-the-world.

Critical gotcha: **listener methods run on the consumer thread.** If your method blocks longer than `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5 minutes), Kafka triggers a rebalance because it thinks the consumer is dead.

In practice, I always set `CooperativeStickyAssignor`, match concurrency to partition count, and keep listener methods fast.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Consumers beyond the partition count sit idle** — `concurrency=8` on a 6-partition topic wastes 2 threads; maximum parallelism equals the partition count.
- **CooperativeStickyAssignor performs incremental rebalances** — only affected partitions are reassigned; other consumers continue processing; default `RangeAssignor` stops all consumers during rebalance.
- **Listener methods run on the consumer thread** — blocking operations prevent the consumer from polling; exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5 minutes) triggers a rebalance.
- **Different groupId values create independent consumers** — each group gets all messages; use separate groups for order processing and analytics reading from the same topic.
- **Manual partition assignment skips group management** — `@TopicPartition(topic, partitions)` assigns fixed partitions; no rebalancing, but no automatic failover if the consumer dies.

questions.question: What are Kafka acknowledgment modes in Spring? When should you use manual acknowledgment?
questions.title: Kafka Acknowledgment Modes — Manual vs Auto
questions.direct_answer: Spring Kafka's AckMode determines when consumer offsets are committed. BATCH (default) commits after each poll batch. MANUAL requires calling Acknowledgment.acknowledge() explicitly, giving full control over exactly when a message is considered processed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of at-least-once delivery and offset commit timing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using auto-commit without realizing messages could be lost if the consumer crashes after commit but before processing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the at-least-once vs at-most-once trade-off and how idempotent consumers handle redelivery

sections.title: Auto-Acknowledge Can Lose Messages — Manual Acknowledge Can Duplicate Them — There Is No Perfect Option
sections.content:
Kafka offset management has a fundamental trade-off: **commit the offset before processing risks losing messages** (if processing fails after commit), and **commit after processing risks duplicates** (if the consumer crashes after processing but before commit). No acknowledgment mode provides exactly-once delivery on its own.

Spring Kafka's default `AckMode.BATCH` commits offsets after all records returned by a single `poll()` are processed. If the listener throws on the third record, the first two are re-delivered on restart because the offset wasn't committed. **This is at-least-once delivery** — messages may be processed more than once but never lost.

`AckMode.RECORD` commits after each individual record. More granular but slower — every commit is a network round-trip to the Kafka broker. For high-throughput topics, the commit overhead becomes significant.

`AckMode.MANUAL` gives full control. The listener receives an `Acknowledgment` parameter and calls `acknowledge()` explicitly. This lets you commit after a database transaction succeeds, ensuring the offset advances only when processing is truly complete.

sections.title: Manual Acknowledgment Patterns and Exactly-Once Considerations
sections.content:
With `MANUAL` mode, inject `Acknowledgment` into the listener method. Call `acknowledgment.acknowledge()` after successful processing. **If you don't call `acknowledge()`, the offset is never committed** — on restart, the consumer re-processes the same messages indefinitely.

`MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` commits the offset as soon as `acknowledge()` is called, without waiting for the next `poll()`. `MANUAL` batches the commit until the next `poll()`. The immediate variant reduces the window for re-delivery on crash but adds commit latency.

For **exactly-once semantics**, use Kafka transactions. The producer and consumer participate in a transaction — the consumed offset is committed in the same transaction as the produced message. Configure `spring.kafka.consumer.properties.isolation.level=read_committed` and enable transactions on the producer. This ensures that offsets and produced messages are committed or rolled back atomically.

sections.content:
Here's the tension most developers miss with Kafka acknowledgment. Commit before processing — message lost if processing fails. Commit after processing — message duplicated if consumer crashes between processing and commit. **No mode gives exactly-once alone.**

Spring Kafka defaults to `AckMode.BATCH` — commits after all records from a single `poll()` are processed. If the listener throws, earlier records are re-delivered. This is at-least-once delivery.

`AckMode.MANUAL` gives full control — inject `Acknowledgment` and call `acknowledge()` after your database transaction succeeds. **If you forget to call it, messages re-process indefinitely.**

For exactly-once, use Kafka transactions — consumed offset and produced messages commit atomically. Set `isolation.level=read_committed`.

Regardless of mode, **make listeners idempotent.** Store a deduplication key and check before processing. This is the pragmatic defense.

In practice, I use `MANUAL` with idempotent listeners for critical data and `BATCH` for analytics/logging where occasional duplicates are acceptable.

sections.title: When a @KafkaListener Throws an Exception, the Default Behavior Is Retry 10 Times Then Log and Move On — The Message Is Lost
sections.content:
The default error handler in Spring Kafka 3.x is `DefaultErrorHandler`. When a listener throws an exception, it retries the failed record up to 10 times with no backoff, then calls a **`ConsumerRecordRecoverer`** — which by default logs the failure and moves on. **The message is effectively lost** after exhausting retries unless you configure a recovery strategy.

The key insight is that Spring Kafka's error handling operates **within a single poll cycle.** The consumer polls a batch of records, processes them sequentially, and if one fails, the error handler retries that record. Other records in the batch wait. This is **blocking retry** — it holds up the consumer thread and can cause the consumer to exceed `max.poll.interval.ms`, triggering a rebalance.

Understanding this default behavior is essential because most developers assume Kafka retries indefinitely or stores failed messages somewhere. It doesn't, unless you configure it. The two production-ready recovery strategies are **Dead Letter Topic (DLT)** publishing and **seek-to-current** (reprocess the same offset until it succeeds).

sections.title: DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer and Custom Error Handlers
sections.content:
**`DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`** publishes the failed record to a Dead Letter Topic (by convention `{original-topic}.DLT`) after retry exhaustion. This preserves the message for later investigation or reprocessing.

Configure it by creating a `DefaultErrorHandler` bean with a custom backoff strategy and a DLT recoverer. `FixedBackOff(1000, 3)` retries 3 times with 1-second intervals. **`ExponentialBackOff`** is better for transient failures — 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s — giving the downstream dependency time to recover.

For specific exception handling, **`addNotRetryableExceptions()`** marks certain exceptions as non-retryable. A `DeserializationException` (poison pill) should never be retried — the message is malformed and will never succeed. Send it directly to the DLT without wasting retry attempts.

For batch listeners (`@KafkaListener` with `batch = "true"`), error handling is different. The entire batch fails or succeeds. If one record fails, the `BatchListenerFailedException` tells Spring Kafka which record failed, and the error handler retries from that record forward.

Retries are **blocking** — they hold the consumer thread within the same poll cycle. If retries take too long, the consumer exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms` and triggers a rebalance.

Two production recovery strategies: **Dead Letter Topic** (publish failed messages to `{topic}.DLT` for later investigation) and **non-blocking retry** (`@RetryableTopic` with separate retry topics).

Mark poison pills (deserialization errors) as **non-retryable** — they'll never succeed. Send directly to DLT.

For batch listeners, `BatchListenerFailedException` identifies which record failed. The handler retries from that record forward.

In practice, I always replace the default handler with `DefaultErrorHandler` using `ExponentialBackOff` and `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`. No message should be silently lost.

sections.title: Blocking Retry Holds Your Consumer Thread — @RetryableTopic Moves Failed Messages to Separate Topics So Processing Continues
sections.content:
The fundamental problem with blocking retry (the default error handler) is that **while one failed record is being retried, no other records on that partition are processed.** If the retry takes 30 seconds (10 retries × 3s backoff), that partition is blocked for 30 seconds. Multiply by partitions and failure frequency, and throughput collapses.

**`@RetryableTopic`** solves this by moving failed messages to separate retry topics: `orders-retry-0`, `orders-retry-1`, `orders-retry-2`, and finally `orders-dlt`. The original consumer immediately moves to the next message. Retry topics have their own consumers that process failed messages after a delay, and if they still fail, the message moves to the next retry topic with a longer delay.

This is **non-blocking retry** — the main consumer is never held up. The delay between retries is achieved by setting the consumer's `poll` interval on retry topics, not by sleeping the thread. After all retry topics are exhausted, the message lands in the DLT for manual intervention.

sections.title: Configuration, Delay Strategies, and When to Use Blocking vs Non-Blocking Retry
sections.content:
Annotate the listener with `@RetryableTopic(attempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2))`. This creates retry topics with delays of 1s, 2s, 4s before the DLT. **Spring Kafka automatically creates the retry and DLT topics** and wires the consumers.

**Fixed delay** retries at the same interval. **Exponential backoff** increases the delay (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s). **The maximum delay should align with your SLA** — if the downstream system's SLA for recovery is 1 hour, your total retry window should match.

Use `@DltHandler` on a method in the same class to define custom DLT processing logic — alerting, storing for manual review, or routing to a human queue.

**Blocking retry is still appropriate for transient failures** where you expect immediate recovery (network blip, momentary lock contention). One or two retries with short backoff is faster than the topic-routing overhead of `@RetryableTopic`. Use non-blocking retry when failures might take minutes or hours to resolve (downstream outage, rate limiting, external API maintenance windows).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Blocking retry holds the consumer thread while retrying. If a record fails 10 times with 3-second backoff, that **partition is blocked for 30 seconds.** No other messages are processed.

`@RetryableTopic` solves this with **non-blocking retry.** Failed messages move to separate retry topics (`orders-retry-0`, `orders-retry-1`) with increasing delays. The original consumer immediately processes the next message.

Configure with `@RetryableTopic(attempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2))`. Spring Kafka creates retry topics and DLT automatically.

After all retry topics are exhausted, the message lands in the DLT. Use `@DltHandler` for custom DLT processing — alerting or storing for manual review.

**Blocking retry is still appropriate for transient failures** — network blips that resolve in milliseconds. Non-blocking retry is for failures that might take minutes to resolve.

In practice, I use blocking retry with 2 attempts for transient errors and `@RetryableTopic` with exponential backoff for downstream outages.

sections.title: Kafka Transactions Solve the 'Consumed But Not Committed' Problem — But They Add Significant Complexity
sections.content:
The classic failure scenario: your consumer reads a message, writes to a database, produces a downstream message, and then crashes before committing the offset. On restart, **the message is consumed again, the database write is duplicated, and the downstream message is sent twice.** Manual acknowledgment alone doesn't prevent this.

Kafka transactions provide **atomicity across consumed offsets and produced messages.** The consumer offset commit and the produced messages are part of the same transaction. If the producer or consumer fails before committing, the entire transaction rolls back — the offset returns to the previous position, and the produced messages are invisible to downstream consumers (with `isolation.level=read_committed`).

Spring Kafka enables transactions by setting `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix`. This activates the `KafkaTransactionManager`, which coordinates the transaction lifecycle. `@Transactional` on a listener method starts a Kafka transaction that includes both the consumed offset and any produced messages. This means either everything commits atomically or nothing does.

sections.title: Configuring Transactions and the Kafka + Database Transaction Coordination Problem
sections.content:
With `transaction-id-prefix` configured, `KafkaTemplate.send()` calls inside a `@Transactional` method participate in the Kafka transaction. The consumed offset is committed as part of the same transaction. If the method throws, both the produced messages and the offset commit are rolled back.

**The challenge is coordinating Kafka transactions with database transactions.** Kafka and your database are separate systems — you can't have a true distributed transaction without a two-phase commit protocol. The practical approach: use `ChainedKafkaTransactionManager` (deprecated in Spring Kafka 3.x) or nest the database transaction inside the Kafka transaction. If the database commit fails, the Kafka transaction rolls back. If the Kafka commit fails after the database commit, you have an inconsistency.

The **Outbox Pattern** is the recommended alternative. Write both the business data and the outbound message to the database in a single ACID transaction. A separate process (CDC with Debezium, or a poller) reads the outbox table and publishes to Kafka. This provides exactly-once semantics without Kafka transactions by leveraging the database's ACID guarantees.

Kafka transactions also require **`isolation.level=read_committed`** on consumers. Without it, consumers see uncommitted messages — messages from transactions that might still roll back.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The failure scenario: consumer reads a message, processes it, produces a downstream message, then crashes before committing the offset. **On restart, everything happens again** — duplicate processing, duplicate downstream messages.

Kafka transactions make consumed offset commit and produced messages **atomic.** Both commit or both roll back. Configure with `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix`.

`@Transactional` on a listener starts a Kafka transaction. Downstream consumers must set **`isolation.level=read_committed`** to avoid reading uncommitted messages.

The hard problem is **Kafka + database coordination.** They're separate systems. If the database commits but the Kafka transaction fails, you have inconsistency.

The **Outbox Pattern** is the recommended solution: write business data and the outbound message to the database in one ACID transaction. A CDC tool (Debezium) publishes to Kafka separately. No Kafka transactions needed.

In practice, I use Kafka transactions for pure consume-transform-produce pipelines and the Outbox Pattern when a database is involved.

sections.content:
- **Kafka transactions make offset commit and produced messages atomic** — both commit or both roll back; prevents the 'consumed but not committed' failure scenario that causes duplicate processing.
- **transaction-id-prefix activates the KafkaTransactionManager** — `KafkaTemplate.send()` inside `@Transactional` participates in the Kafka transaction; offset commit is part of the same transaction.
- **isolation.level=read_committed is required on downstream consumers** — without it, consumers see messages from transactions that might roll back; leads to processing uncommitted and eventually rolled-back data.
- **Kafka + database coordination requires the Outbox Pattern** — write business data and outbound messages to the database in one ACID transaction; CDC (Debezium) publishes to Kafka; avoids distributed transaction complexity.
- **ChainedKafkaTransactionManager is deprecated in Spring Kafka 3.x** — nesting database transactions inside Kafka transactions is fragile; the Outbox Pattern provides stronger consistency guarantees.

sections.title: JSON Is Human-Readable But Has No Schema Contract — Avro Is Compact, Schema-Enforced, and Enables Evolution
sections.content:
Most teams start with JSON because it's familiar and readable. Then the consumer breaks because a producer added a field. The choice between JSON and Avro isn't just about format — it's about **whether the producer and consumer agree on the message structure.**

JSON (`JsonSerializer`/`JsonDeserializer`) is simple and human-readable. But it has no schema enforcement — the producer can add, remove, or change fields without the consumer knowing. The consumer discovers incompatibilities at runtime with `ClassCastException` or missing fields. JSON also includes field names in every message, making messages significantly larger.

**Avro** encodes data with a schema that defines the structure. The schema is registered in a **Schema Registry** (Confluent). Producers and consumers reference the schema by ID, not by embedding it in every message. This means messages are **compact** (only values, no field names) and **schema-enforced** (the registry validates compatibility before allowing changes). Avro supports **schema evolution** — adding an optional field doesn't break existing consumers.

sections.title: JSON vs Avro — Size, Schema, and Evolution Trade-offs
sections.content:
The trade-off is simplicity vs governance.

| Aspect | JSON | Avro |
|---|---|---|
| **Readability** | Human-readable | Binary (not readable) |
| **Message size** | Large (includes field names) | Compact (schema ID + values only) |
| **Schema** | None — implicit in code | Explicit — registered in Schema Registry |
| **Evolution** | No guarantees — runtime failures | Controlled — forward/backward compatibility checks |
| **Setup** | Zero infrastructure | Requires Schema Registry |
| **Debugging** | Easy — read raw messages | Requires schema to decode |
| **Spring config** | `JsonSerializer`/`JsonDeserializer` | `KafkaAvroSerializer`/`KafkaAvroDeserializer` |

**Use JSON** for internal tools, prototyping, and low-throughput topics where readability matters. **Use Avro** for production event-driven systems where multiple teams consume the same topics, schema governance is needed, and message volume makes size matter.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JSON is simple and human-readable, but it has **no schema contract.** The producer can change fields without the consumer knowing. Incompatibilities show up at runtime.

Avro encodes data with an explicit schema registered in a Schema Registry. Messages are **compact** (schema ID + values, no field names) and **schema-enforced** (the registry validates compatibility before allowing changes).

Avro supports **schema evolution** — adding an optional field with a default doesn't break existing consumers. Forward and backward compatibility checks happen at registration time, not at runtime.

The trade-off: Avro requires Schema Registry infrastructure. JSON requires nothing.

In Spring Kafka, configure `KafkaAvroSerializer` and point to the Schema Registry URL. For JSON, `JsonSerializer` with `JsonDeserializer` works with no infrastructure.

My recommendation: JSON for prototyping and internal tools. Avro for production event-driven architectures where multiple teams consume the same topics and schema governance matters.

sections.content:

sections.title: @EmbeddedKafka Starts a Real Kafka Broker in the Test JVM — No Docker, No External Dependencies
sections.content:
Testing Kafka consumers and producers requires a running Kafka broker. **`@EmbeddedKafka`** starts an in-memory Kafka broker inside the test JVM — real Kafka, not a mock. Your producer sends real messages, your consumer receives them through the actual Kafka protocol. This catches serialization issues, partition behavior, and consumer group mechanics that mocks would miss.

Add `spring-kafka-test` dependency and annotate the test class with `@EmbeddedKafka(partitions = 3, topics = {"test-orders"})`. Spring Boot auto-configures the embedded broker and sets `spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers` to the embedded broker's address.

The challenge with Kafka tests is **asynchronicity.** The producer sends a message, but the consumer processes it on a separate thread. You can't assert immediately after sending. Use **`ConsumerRecord` assertions with timeouts** — `KafkaTestUtils.getRecords(consumer, Duration.ofSeconds(10))` polls until records arrive or the timeout expires. For listener-based tests, use `CountDownLatch` or `Awaitility` to wait for the listener to process the message.

sections.title: Testing Producers, Consumers, and Error Handling Scenarios
sections.content:
**Producer tests** send a message with `KafkaTemplate` and verify it arrives using a test consumer created from `ConsumerFactory`. Assert on the record's key, value, headers, and partition. This validates serialization configuration and partition routing.

**Consumer tests** produce a message using `KafkaTemplate` or a test producer and assert that the `@KafkaListener` method processed it. Inject a `CountDownLatch` into the listener and `await()` in the test. This validates deserialization, consumer group assignment, and listener logic.

**Error handling tests** verify that failed messages reach the DLT. Send a message that causes the listener to throw, wait for retries to exhaust, and assert that a record appears on the DLT topic. This validates the entire error-handling pipeline: retry, backoff, and recovery.

For **unique topic names per test**, append `@DynamicPropertySource` or use `UUID.randomUUID()` in topic names. Shared topics between test methods cause interference — one test consumes another test's messages, leading to flaky tests.

For producer tests: send with `KafkaTemplate`, consume with a test consumer, assert on key/value/partition.

For consumer tests: produce a test message, wait for the `@KafkaListener` to process it via `CountDownLatch`.

For error handling tests: send a message that causes failure, verify it reaches the DLT after retries.

In practice, I use `@EmbeddedKafka` for integration tests and Testcontainers with a real Kafka container for more realistic end-to-end tests.

questions.question: What triggers a Kafka consumer group rebalance? How do you minimize rebalance impact?
questions.title: Consumer Group Rebalancing — Causes and Mitigation
questions.direct_answer: Rebalancing is triggered when consumers join or leave the group (scaling, restarts, crashes) or when a consumer misses heartbeats. During rebalancing, all consumers in the group stop consuming. Minimize with static membership, session.timeout tuning, and cooperative rebalancing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of rebalancing as a production reliability concern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that long processing times (exceeding max.poll.interval.ms) trigger rebalance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain cooperative incremental rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+) and static membership as alternatives to eager rebalancing

sections.title: Every Time a Consumer Joins or Leaves a Group, All Consumers Pause — This Is Why Rolling Deployments Cause Latency Spikes
sections.content:
A Kafka consumer group rebalance reassigns partitions among consumers. During rebalance, **all consumers in the group stop processing** until the assignment is complete. No messages are consumed. For high-throughput topics, even a 30-second rebalance window causes significant message lag.

Rebalances are triggered by: a consumer joining the group (scaling up, deployment), a consumer leaving (scaling down, crash, exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms`), a consumer's `session.timeout.ms` expiring (missed heartbeats), or a topic partition count change.

**Rolling deployments are the most common trigger** in production. Each instance restart causes a leave-then-join, triggering two rebalances per instance. With 10 instances, a rolling deployment triggers up to 20 rebalances. The mitigation is `group.instance.id` — **static membership** — which gives each consumer a stable identity. When a consumer with a static ID restarts, it reclaims its partitions without triggering a full rebalance, as long as it returns within `session.timeout.ms`.

sections.title: Cooperative Rebalancing and Static Membership — Reducing the Impact
sections.content:
The default **eager rebalancing protocol** revokes all partitions from all consumers and reassigns them from scratch. Even if only one partition needs to move, every consumer stops.

**Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing** (`CooperativeStickyAssignor`) only moves the affected partitions. Consumers that keep their partitions continue processing without interruption. This dramatically reduces the impact of rebalances during scaling or deployments.

**Static membership** (`group.instance.id`) assigns a stable identity to each consumer. Configure a unique, stable ID per instance (e.g., hostname or pod name). When the consumer restarts and reconnects with the same ID, the broker reassigns its previous partitions immediately — no rebalance notification to other consumers. Set `session.timeout.ms` high enough to cover your deployment window (e.g., 5 minutes).

**Combine both strategies** for production: cooperative rebalancing for minimal disruption when partitions do move, and static membership to avoid triggering rebalances during rolling deployments entirely. Monitor consumer group lag during deployments to verify the impact.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Every consumer group rebalance **stops all consumers from processing** until partitions are reassigned. Rolling deployments are the most common trigger — each instance restart causes leave + join, potentially 20 rebalances for a 10-instance deployment.

Three strategies to reduce impact:

**Cooperative rebalancing** (`CooperativeStickyAssignor`) only moves affected partitions. Other consumers keep processing. The default eager protocol stops everyone.

**Static membership** (`group.instance.id`) gives each consumer a stable identity. On restart, it reclaims its partitions without triggering a full rebalance. Set `session.timeout.ms` high enough to cover your deployment window.

**Combine both** for production — cooperative rebalancing for minimal disruption when partitions move, static membership to avoid rebalances during deployments entirely.

Monitor consumer lag during deployments to verify the impact.

In practice, I always configure `CooperativeStickyAssignor` and `group.instance.id` for production consumers. The difference between a smooth deployment and a lag spike is these two settings.

- **Rolling deployments trigger up to 2 rebalances per instance** — leave (stop) and join (start); 10 instances = up to 20 rebalances; each one pauses all consumers.
- **CooperativeStickyAssignor performs incremental rebalancing** — only affected partitions are reassigned; other consumers continue processing without interruption.
- **Static membership (group.instance.id) avoids rebalance on restart** — consumer reclaims its previous partitions if it reconnects within `session.timeout.ms`; set timeout high enough to cover deployment window.
- **Exceeding max.poll.interval.ms triggers a rebalance** — long-running listener processing makes the broker think the consumer is dead; increase the interval or process faster.

questions.question: How do you optimize Kafka producer throughput with batching and compression?
questions.title: Kafka Producer Throughput — Batching and Compression
questions.direct_answer: Kafka producers batch messages before sending. Tune linger.ms (wait time to fill batch) and batch.size (max bytes). Add snappy or lz4 compression for 3-5x payload reduction. These are the highest-impact producer throughput settings.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of producer throughput tuning at the configuration level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting linger.ms=0 (default) for low-latency use cases while also needing high throughput — the two goals are in tension
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that linger.ms and batch.size are independent limits — whichever triggers first sends the batch

sections.title: Kafka Producers Don't Send Messages Immediately — They Batch Them, and the Tuning Determines Your Latency-Throughput Trade-off
sections.content:
When you call `KafkaTemplate.send()`, the message doesn't go to the broker immediately. It's added to a **per-partition buffer** in the producer. The buffer is flushed when either the **batch is full** (`batch.size`, default 16KB) or the **linger time expires** (`linger.ms`, default 0ms). With default settings, messages are sent almost immediately because `linger.ms=0` triggers a send as soon as any message is in the buffer.

Increasing `linger.ms` (e.g., to 5-20ms) allows more messages to accumulate in the batch, reducing the number of network round-trips. This **increases latency** (each message waits up to `linger.ms` before sending) but dramatically **improves throughput** (fewer, larger network requests).

**Compression** (`compression.type`) compresses each batch before sending. `lz4` provides the best balance of compression ratio and CPU overhead. `snappy` is faster but compresses less. `gzip` compresses the most but uses the most CPU. Compression is applied per-batch, so larger batches compress more efficiently — another reason to increase `linger.ms`.

sections.title: Tuning for Throughput vs Latency — Production Configurations
sections.content:
For **low-latency** scenarios (real-time event processing): `linger.ms=0` (default), `batch.size=16384` (default). Messages send immediately. Throughput is lower because each send is a separate network request.

For **high-throughput** scenarios (log aggregation, analytics): `linger.ms=20`, `batch.size=65536` (64KB), `compression.type=lz4`. Messages batch for up to 20ms, producing larger, compressed batches. Network requests drop by 10-50x.

**`buffer.memory`** (default 32MB) is the total memory available for all buffers. If the producer generates messages faster than the broker accepts them, buffers fill up. When `buffer.memory` is exhausted, `send()` blocks for up to `max.block.ms` (default 60 seconds) and then throws `TimeoutException`.

Monitor the `record-queue-time-avg` metric — it shows how long messages wait in the buffer before sending. High values indicate that `linger.ms` is too high or the broker is slow. Monitor `batch-size-avg` to verify that batches are being filled effectively. A batch-size-avg much smaller than `batch.size` means `linger.ms` is flushing before batches are full.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kafka producers batch messages instead of sending them individually. `send()` adds the message to a per-partition buffer. The buffer flushes when the **batch is full** (`batch.size`, default 16KB) or the **linger time expires** (`linger.ms`, default 0ms).

With `linger.ms=0`, messages send almost immediately — low latency, lower throughput. Setting `linger.ms=20` lets messages accumulate, producing larger batches with fewer network round-trips.

**Compression** (`lz4` is the best default) compresses each batch before sending. Larger batches compress more efficiently — another reason to increase `linger.ms`.

For high throughput: `linger.ms=20`, `batch.size=65536`, `compression.type=lz4`. Network requests drop 10-50x.

`buffer.memory` (default 32MB) is the total producer buffer. When exhausted, `send()` blocks and eventually throws `TimeoutException`.

In practice, I always set `compression.type=lz4` and tune `linger.ms` based on latency requirements — 5ms for near-real-time, 20ms for analytics.

sections.content:
- **linger.ms=0 (default) sends messages immediately** — lowest latency but highest network overhead; setting 5-20ms lets messages batch, reducing network round-trips by 10-50x.

- **lz4 provides the best compression-to-CPU ratio** — snappy is faster but compresses less; gzip compresses more but uses significantly more CPU; compression is per-batch, so larger batches compress better.

- **Monitor record-queue-time-avg and batch-size-avg** — high queue time indicates linger.ms is too high or broker is slow; batch-size-avg much smaller than batch.size means linger.ms flushes before batches fill.

questions.question: How do you monitor and alert on Kafka consumer lag?
questions.title: Kafka Consumer Lag Monitoring and Alerting
questions.direct_answer: Consumer lag (difference between latest offset and consumer position) indicates how far behind consumers are. Monitor via Kafka AdminClient, Confluent Control Center, or export to Prometheus with kafka-lag-exporter. Alert when lag consistently grows.

interviewer_intent.testing: Operational awareness of Kafka consumer health monitoring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Alerting on absolute lag value instead of lag trend — a constant lag is acceptable, growing lag is not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between a lag spike (burst of messages) and a processing throughput issue, and how to diagnose each

sections.title: Consumer Lag Is the Gap Between What's Produced and What's Consumed — If It Grows, Your System Is Falling Behind
sections.content:
Consumer lag measures the difference between the **log-end offset** (latest message in the partition) and the **committed offset** (last message the consumer confirmed processing). A lag of 0 means the consumer is fully caught up. Growing lag means the consumer is processing slower than the producer is writing.

Lag is the **most important Kafka operational metric.** It directly indicates whether your system is keeping up with incoming data. A consumer that's 1 million messages behind on an order topic means 1 million unprocessed orders. The lag number doesn't tell you the time delay — that depends on the production rate. If the producer writes 10,000 messages/second, a lag of 1 million means approximately 100 seconds behind.

Kafka provides lag data through the **`kafka-consumer-groups.sh` CLI tool** and through **JMX metrics** exposed by the consumer client. Spring Boot Actuator with Micrometer exposes consumer metrics at the `kafka.consumer.*` namespace. For production monitoring, **Burrow** (LinkedIn's open-source tool) evaluates lag trends and alerts on consumers that are falling behind rather than just on absolute lag values.

sections.title: Monitoring Strategies, Alerting, and Root Cause Analysis
sections.content:
**Absolute lag alerts** trigger when lag exceeds a threshold (e.g., 10,000 messages). This catches sudden spikes but doesn't account for temporary bursts that the consumer will catch up on. **Lag trend alerts** (Burrow's approach) trigger when lag is consistently growing over time — the consumer is falling further behind, not just temporarily spiked.

Common root causes for growing lag: **slow listener processing** (database writes, HTTP calls blocking the consumer thread), **insufficient concurrency** (fewer consumers than partitions), **frequent rebalances** (during which no messages are processed), **GC pauses** (long pauses cause the consumer to miss poll deadlines).

To diagnose, check the **consumer's `records-consumed-rate`** and **`records-lag`** metrics. If consumed-rate is low but lag is high, the consumer is slow. If consumed-rate matches production rate but lag remains high, the consumer was behind and is catching up.

For Kubernetes, **scale consumers horizontally** based on lag. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) scales consumer deployments based on Kafka consumer lag — adding pods when lag exceeds a threshold and scaling down when the consumer catches up.

Monitor lag via JMX metrics, Spring Boot Actuator (`kafka.consumer.*`), or Burrow (LinkedIn's tool that evaluates lag trends, not just absolute values).

- **Lag trend is more important than absolute lag** — a temporary spike during a burst is normal; consistently growing lag indicates a systemic problem; Burrow evaluates trends.
- **Slow listener processing is the most common cause** — blocking operations (database writes, HTTP calls) hold the consumer thread; optimize processing time or increase concurrency.
- **Insufficient concurrency means idle partitions** — if you have 12 partitions but concurrency=3, each consumer handles 4 partitions sequentially; increase concurrency up to the partition count.
- **KEDA auto-scales Kafka consumers in Kubernetes based on lag** — adds pods when lag exceeds a threshold, scales down when caught up; eliminates manual scaling decisions.

beats.text: Consumer lag measures the difference between the log-end offset (latest message in the partition) and the committed offset (last message the consumer confirmed processing). A lag of 0 means the consumer is fully caught up. Growing lag means the consumer is processing slower than the producer is writing. Lag is the most important Kafka operational metric. It directly indicates whether your system is keeping up with incoming data. A consumer that's 1 million messages behind on an order topic means 1 million unprocessed orders. The lag number doesn't tell you.

steps: Absolute lag alerts trigger when lag exceeds a threshold (e.g., 10,000 messages).
This catches sudden spikes but doesn't account for temporary bursts that the consumer will catch up on.
Lag trend alerts (Burrow's approach) trigger when lag is consistently growing over time — the consumer is falling further behind, not just temporarily spiked.

Common root causes for growing lag: slow listener processing (database writes, HTTP calls blocking the consumer thread), insufficient concurrency (fewer consumers than partitions), frequent rebalances (during which no messages are processed), GC pauses (long pauses cause the consumer to miss poll deadlines).
To diagnose, check the consumer's records-consumed-rate and records-lag metrics.
If consumed-rate is low but lag is high, the consumer is slow.

Lag trend is more important than absolute lag — a temporary spike during a burst is normal; consistently growing lag indicates a systemic problem; Burrow evaluates trends
Slow listener processing is the most common cause — blocking operations (database writes, HTTP calls) hold the consumer thread; optimize processing time or increase concurrency
Insufficient concurrency means idle partitions — if you have 12 partitions but concurrency=3, each consumer handles 4 partitions sequentially; increase concurrency up to the partition count
KEDA auto-scales Kafka consumers in Kubernetes based on lag — adds pods when lag exceeds a threshold, scales down when caught up; eliminates manual scaling decisions

questions.title: Kafka Message Headers — Metadata and Context Propagation
questions.direct_answer: Kafka message headers are key-value byte pairs attached to each message. Spring Kafka uses them internally (type info, trace IDs) and exposes them via @Header in listeners. Use them for correlation IDs, event versioning, and distributed tracing context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Kafka headers for cross-cutting concerns without polluting message payloads
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting metadata like correlationId and eventVersion inside the message payload instead of headers

sections.title: Kafka Headers Are Metadata Attached to Messages — Use Them for Tracing, Routing, and Schema IDs Without Polluting the Payload
sections.content:
Kafka headers are key-value pairs attached to each record, separate from the key and value. They carry metadata without modifying the message payload. Common use cases: **trace IDs** for distributed tracing, **correlation IDs** for request tracking, **schema version** for deserialization, **content type** for format detection, and **source service** for audit trails.

Spring Kafka's `KafkaTemplate` supports headers through `ProducerRecord` or `MessageBuilder`. `Message<OrderEvent> message = MessageBuilder.withPayload(event).setHeader("X-Trace-Id", traceId).build(); kafkaTemplate.send(message);` attaches the trace ID as a header.

On the consumer side, `@Header("X-Trace-Id") String traceId` extracts a specific header, or inject `ConsumerRecordMetadata` to access all headers. Spring Kafka's `DefaultKafkaHeaderMapper` automatically maps Spring `Message` headers to Kafka headers and back.

Headers are particularly useful for **dead letter topic processing** — Spring Kafka automatically adds headers to DLT records containing the original topic, partition, offset, exception class, and exception message. This metadata is essential for debugging and reprocessing failed messages.

sections.title: Common Header Patterns and the KafkaHeaderMapper
sections.content:
**Distributed tracing headers** propagate trace context across Kafka boundaries. Micrometer Tracing automatically adds `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers to produced messages and extracts them on the consumer side. This enables end-to-end tracing across HTTP and Kafka without manual header management.

**Routing headers** enable consumers to filter or route messages without deserializing the payload. A `Content-Type` header can tell the consumer whether the payload is JSON, Avro, or Protobuf. A `Message-Type` header (e.g., `OrderCreated`, `OrderCancelled`) enables a single listener to dispatch to different handlers based on the event type.

`DefaultKafkaHeaderMapper` handles conversion between Spring `MessageHeaders` and Kafka `Headers`. It serializes non-`byte[]` header values to JSON automatically. **Be careful with header size** — headers count toward the message size limit (`max.message.bytes`, default 1MB). Large headers reduce the space available for the actual payload.

For custom header filtering on the consumer side, implement a `RecordFilterStrategy` that inspects headers before the message reaches the listener. This avoids deserializing messages that the consumer doesn't need.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kafka headers carry metadata **separate from the payload** — trace IDs, correlation IDs, content types, source service names. They avoid polluting the message body with infrastructure concerns.

In Spring Kafka, use `MessageBuilder.withPayload(event).setHeader("X-Trace-Id", traceId).build()` to attach headers. On the consumer side, `@Header("X-Trace-Id") String traceId` extracts them.

Micrometer Tracing **automatically propagates trace context** via headers — `traceparent` and `tracestate` added on produce, extracted on consume. End-to-end tracing across HTTP and Kafka without manual management.

Spring Kafka adds **DLT headers automatically** — original topic, partition, offset, exception class, and message. Essential for debugging failed messages.

Headers count toward the message size limit (`max.message.bytes`, default 1MB). Keep them small.

In practice, I use headers for trace IDs, event type routing, and correlation IDs. The payload stays clean with only business data.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Headers carry metadata without modifying the payload** — trace IDs, correlation IDs, schema versions, and content types stay separate from business data; consumers can inspect headers without deserializing.
- **Micrometer Tracing propagates trace context via headers automatically** — `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers enable end-to-end distributed tracing across HTTP and Kafka boundaries.
- **Spring Kafka adds DLT headers with failure details** — original topic, partition, offset, exception class, and message; essential for debugging and reprocessing dead letter records.
- **Headers count toward max.message.bytes (default 1MB)** — large headers reduce space for the payload; keep metadata small; use header references (IDs) instead of embedding large values.
- **RecordFilterStrategy can filter messages by header before deserialization** — avoids deserializing messages the consumer doesn't need; improves throughput for consumers that process only specific event types.
